title: Order API latency spike
content: P95 latency increased significantly. The incident began shortly after the latest deployment. Engineers noticed response times exceeding 8 seconds. On-call team was paged at 02:15 UTC. Downstream services including checkout and fulfillment were impacted. Rolling back the deployment was considered but not executed pending investigation.

title: Orders deployment v2.8.1
content: Version v2.8.1 was deployed to production at 18:10 UTC. Changes included a new connection pool configuration and updated ORM query patterns for the order history endpoint. Deployment was performed using blue-green strategy. No issues observed immediately post-deployment. Smoke tests passed. Database migration scripts ran successfully.

title: Previous latency incident postmortem
content: A previous latency incident was caused by database connection saturation during a schema migration. The migration script held locks on the orders table for longer than anticipated, causing connection pool exhaustion. Fix involved increasing pool size and adding a migration lock timeout. Recommended adding pre-migration load tests before future schema changes.

title: Service restart procedure
content: Restart Service A when latency remains high for more than 5 minutes and there is no active downstream dependency failure. This procedure applies to general latency scenarios not caused by an upstream dependency outage. Steps: 1. Confirm latency spike via metrics dashboard. 2. Check for active alerts from downstream services. 3. If no downstream alerts, initiate graceful restart via deployment tool.

title: Service A incident procedure for dependency failures
content: Do not restart Service A during dependency failures. Check dependency health first. Restarting during an active dependency failure will cause connection storm and worsen the incident. Procedure: 1. Check dependency health dashboard. 2. If any upstream or downstream dependency is unhealthy, do NOT restart. 3. Coordinate with the owning team to resolve dependency before any restart. This supersedes GUIDE-12 only when a dependency failure is detected. GUIDE-12 still applies for isolated latency scenarios.

title: Catalog latency
content: Latency increased due to database saturation. The catalog search endpoint experienced p99 latency exceeding 12 seconds. Root cause identified as database connection saturation caused by a sudden spike in read-heavy queries triggered by a marketing campaign. No deployment preceded this incident. Database read replicas were scaled up to resolve.

title: Order errors
content: Requests failed because of an expired certificate. The TLS certificate for the orders-api to payments-api mutual authentication expired at 00:01 UTC. This caused all order placement requests that required payment authorization to fail with connection errors. Root cause: certificate renewal process was not automated. Fix: automated certificate renewal via cert-manager was implemented.

title: Order API latency — TLS handshake failure
content: Orders API experienced severe latency spike. Investigation revealed the root cause was TLS certificate expiry for the internal gRPC channel between orders-api and inventory-service. Latency was caused by repeated TLS handshake failures triggering retry storms, NOT by database issues. This incident is superficially similar to DB saturation incidents but has a fundamentally different root cause. Resolved by emergency certificate renewal.

title: Order API latency — memory leak
content: Sustained latency increase over 72 hours. Root cause was a memory leak introduced in v2.5.0 in the order history cache module. As heap usage grew, garbage collection pauses caused increasing latency spikes. Not related to database connections or deployments in this window. Fix: patched cache eviction logic, deployed as hotfix v2.5.1.

title: Postmortem — TLS certificate expiry incident Aug 2025
content: Root cause confirmed as TLS certificate expiry. Latency symptoms appeared identical to DB saturation incidents but mechanism was entirely different. Engineers initially suspected database issues due to similar surface symptoms. Key differentiator: DB connection pool metrics were normal; TLS error logs showed handshake failures. Recommendation: add certificate expiry monitoring with 30-day alert threshold.

title: Postmortem — memory leak incident Nov 2024
content: Memory leak in order history cache module was the root cause of the Nov 2024 latency incident. Heap profiling revealed unbounded cache growth. Database metrics were normal throughout. This is distinct from the May 2026 DB saturation incident (PM-211). Recommendation: add heap memory alerting at 80% threshold, enforce cache TTLs.

title: Inventory service database connection saturation
content: Inventory service experienced DB connection saturation during a schema migration for the warehouse_items table. Symptoms were nearly identical to the orders-api DB saturation incident (PM-211) — connection pool exhaustion, cascading timeouts. However this is a completely separate service with its own database cluster. Root cause: same pattern (migration lock contention) but on inventory-service infrastructure. Fixed by aborting migration and scheduling during off-peak hours.

title: Inventory service DB saturation postmortem
content: DB connection saturation on inventory-service during schema migration mirrors the pattern seen in orders-api PM-211 but is a distinct incident on a different service with separate infrastructure. The shared pattern suggests a systemic problem with migration procedures across teams. Recommendation: standardize pre-migration checklist including connection pool analysis, to be applied company-wide.

title: Payments API database connection saturation
content: Payments API DB connection pool saturated during high-traffic Black Friday preparation load test. Root cause: connection pool size was not scaled before load test. Distinct from orders-api incidents — payments-api has its own RDS instance. No deployment preceded this. Fixed by emergency pool size increase.

title: Orders API restart procedure (deprecated)
content: DEPRECATED — superseded by GUIDE-12 and GUIDE-41. Original procedure: immediately restart orders-api on any latency alert. This procedure is outdated and should not be followed. It was written before dependency health checks were implemented and does not account for dependency failure scenarios. Kept for historical reference only.

title: High memory restart procedure
content: Restart the affected service when heap memory usage exceeds 90% and latency is degraded. This procedure applies specifically to memory-pressure scenarios. Do not use this procedure for latency caused by DB connection issues or dependency failures. Memory-triggered restarts should be followed by a heap dump for postmortem analysis. This is complementary to GUIDE-12 and GUIDE-41, not a replacement. All three may apply under different conditions.

title: Orders API DB connection pool runbook
content: When orders-api DB connection pool is saturated: 1. Do NOT restart the service — this drops all active connections and worsens the situation immediately. 2. Increase pool_max_size via runtime config API without restart. 3. Check for active schema migrations via DBA console. 4. If migration is running, coordinate with DBA to assess lock duration. 5. Alert: This procedure does not apply if the saturation is caused by query volume (not migrations) — in that case, add read replicas.

title: Certificate expiry incident response
content: When a TLS certificate expiry is identified as the root cause of service failure: 1. Initiate emergency cert renewal via cert-manager CLI. 2. Do NOT restart the service before cert renewal — restart without a valid cert will cause immediate connection failures. 3. After cert renewal, perform rolling restart to pick up new cert. 4. Verify handshake success via openssl s_client check. This procedure is specific to certificate expiry scenarios and does not apply to latency caused by DB or memory issues.

title: Orders API v2.8.0 deployment
content: Version v2.8.0 deployed to production at 14:30 UTC. Changes: upgraded ORM library from 3.x to 4.x, added order analytics endpoint, refactored connection pooling to use async pool. Smoke tests passed. DB migration ran cleanly. No incidents in 24h post-deployment window.

title: Orders API v2.7.9 deployment
content: Hotfix deployment v2.7.9 at 09:00 UTC. Addresses race condition in order status update handler. No DB schema changes. No incidents observed post-deployment.

title: Orders API v2.7.8 deployment
content: Version v2.7.8 deployed at 11:00 UTC. Added new order export API. Updated logging configuration. No DB schema changes. Deployment was uneventful.

title: Orders API v2.8.1 rollback assessment
content: Following the Sep 16 latency spike (INC-1042), rollback of v2.8.1 to v2.8.0 was evaluated. Decision was made to investigate root cause before rolling back. DB connection pool metrics showed saturation pattern consistent with prior incidents. Rollback was held pending DBA analysis of connection pool config change in v2.8.1.

title: Customer complaint — slow checkout Sep 16
content: Multiple enterprise customers reported checkout process hanging for over 10 seconds starting around 02:30 UTC on September 16. One customer reported 47 failed order attempts. SLA breach notification triggered for 3 enterprise accounts. Complaints routed to engineering oncall.

title: Customer complaint — order placement failures Jul 12
content: Customers unable to place orders between 00:01 and 04:30 UTC on July 12. Error messages showed payment authorization failures. Approximately 1,200 orders failed. Root cause was certificate expiry (INC-301). Customers offered credit for inconvenience.

title: Customer complaint — slow search Jul 11
content: Search results took over 15 seconds to load throughout July 11. Customers reported inability to browse product catalog. Mapped to catalog-api latency incident INC-300. Database saturation caused by marketing campaign traffic spike.

title: Orders API architecture overview
content: Orders API is a Python FastAPI service backed by PostgreSQL 15. Uses SQLAlchemy with asyncpg connection pool (default pool_max_size=10). Depends on: payments-api (mTLS gRPC), inventory-service (REST), notification-service (async queue). DB schema migrations managed by Alembic. Connection pool is shared across all worker threads — saturation risk during heavy migrations or traffic spikes. Service discovery via Consul.

title: Catalog API architecture overview
content: Catalog API is a Go service backed by PostgreSQL 15 read replicas. Designed for high-read workloads. Write path goes through primary; read path uses read replicas with connection pooling via PgBouncer. Elasticsearch is used for full-text search. During marketing campaigns, read replica count should be pre-scaled. Known risk: if read replicas lag, queries fall back to primary causing saturation.

title: Payments API architecture overview
content: Payments API is a Java Spring Boot service. Uses HikariCP connection pool. Connects to orders-api via mTLS. TLS certificates are managed by cert-manager with 90-day rotation. Critical: certificate rotation is automated but requires orders-api and payments-api to be restarted within the renewal window to pick up new certs. If rotation is missed, mTLS handshake fails causing payment authorization failures.

title: Auth service architecture overview
content: Auth service handles OAuth2 and JWT issuance. Backed by Redis for session storage and PostgreSQL for user data. Issues JWT tokens with 1-hour expiry. Known issue: if Redis becomes unavailable, auth falls back to DB-only mode causing significant latency increase on login endpoints. Rate limiting is applied at the API gateway layer, not within auth-service itself.

title: Inventory service architecture overview
content: Inventory service manages warehouse stock levels. PostgreSQL 14 backend. Schema migrations run via Flyway. Known risk: Flyway migrations on the warehouse_items table (large table, ~50M rows) can hold locks for extended periods causing connection pool saturation. Recommend running large migrations during maintenance windows with reduced traffic.

title: Pre-deployment discussion for v2.8.1
content: Thread: Team discussed risks of the connection pool config change in v2.8.1. @alice: 'The new pool config increases max connections to 25 — should we load test first?' @bob: 'Load test was run in staging but not under migration conditions.' @carol: 'v2.8.1 also changes ORM query patterns which could affect pool behavior.' Decision: proceed with deployment, monitor pool metrics post-deploy. No pre-migration load test was conducted.

title: Post-incident discussion — Sep 16 latency spike
content: Thread post INC-1042: @alice: 'Pool exhaustion pattern matches PM-211 almost exactly — same saturation under migration conditions.' @bob: 'But the migration in v2.8.1 was smaller than the PM-211 migration — why did it saturate?' @carol: 'The new ORM query patterns generate more connections per transaction. The migration + new query patterns combined overwhelmed the pool.' Conclusion: root cause is interaction between pool config change and ORM query changes, triggered during migration.

title: Auth service — certificate expiry incident
content: Auth service internal certificates expired, causing login failures for approximately 2 hours. Root cause: internal mTLS certificate between auth-service and Redis cluster expired. Symptoms: login requests timing out, JWT issuance failures. This is a certificate expiry incident similar in mechanism to INC-301 (orders-api) but on a completely different service and certificate pair. Resolved by emergency cert renewal.

title: Auth service — DB saturation under load
content: Auth service database connections saturated during a load test gone wrong in production. Login endpoint p99 exceeded 20 seconds. Root cause: DB connection pool exhaustion caused by an unthrottled load test consuming all available connections. Note: same pattern as orders-api DB saturation (PM-211) but entirely separate service and infrastructure. Fixed by terminating the load test and restarting connection pool.

title: Auth service certificate expiry postmortem
content: Certificate expiry caused 2-hour auth outage. Root cause: cert-manager rotation job failed silently due to a namespace permission error introduced in a Kubernetes RBAC update. The same silent-failure pattern was identified in payments-api cert rotation (ARCH-03). Recommendation: add explicit cert expiry monitoring across all services, not just orders-api and payments-api.

title: Auth service v5.9.0 deployment
content: Auth service v5.9.0 deployed at 10:00 UTC. Changes: new OAuth2 PKCE flow, Kubernetes RBAC update for cert-manager namespace permissions. Deployment proceeded without issues. Note: the RBAC change introduced a namespace permission error that caused cert-manager rotation to fail silently — discovered 4 days later during the certificate expiry incident (INC-400).

title: Payments API timeout following load test
content: Payments API timeouts started immediately after a Black Friday load test. Root cause: DB connection pool was not returned to baseline settings after the load test. The pool was configured for load test concurrency levels and caused resource contention in production. Different from DB saturation due to migrations — this is saturation from excessive pool size vs. actual DB capacity.

title: Payments API — 503 errors under memory pressure
content: Payments API began returning 503 errors after JVM heap reached 95%. Root cause: memory leak in payment retry queue handler. As memory pressure increased, GC pauses caused request timeouts leading to 503s. Different from DB or certificate issues. Resolved by restarting service after heap dump capture. Hotfix deployed as v3.9.1.

title: Payments API memory leak postmortem
content: Memory leak in payment retry queue accumulated unbounded retry objects when external payment provider was slow. Fix: added bounded queue with max retry limit. Heap profiling confirmed memory was released after fix. Pattern similar to orders-api memory leak (PM-213) but in a completely different module and service.

title: Payments API v4.1.0 deployment
content: Payments API v4.1.0 deployed at 15:00 UTC. Key changes: upgraded HikariCP pool library, increased default pool_max_size from 10 to 20, added circuit breaker for payment provider calls. Smoke tests passed. No DB schema migrations. Deployment uneventful.

title: Customer complaint — payment failures Oct 14
content: Dozens of customers reported checkout errors showing 'Service Unavailable' when attempting payment. Payments API was returning 503 due to memory pressure (INC-501). Estimated revenue impact: $45,000. Customers offered refund of any processing fees.

title: Catalog API v5.1 deployment
content: Catalog API v5.1 deployed at 09:00 UTC on July 10. Changes: new product filtering API, Elasticsearch index mapping update, read replica connection pool tuning. No incidents immediately post-deployment. Marketing campaign started July 11 triggered unexpected traffic spike leading to INC-300.

title: Catalog API — index corruption postmortem Dec 2025
content: Catalog API latency incident in Dec 2025 was caused by Elasticsearch index corruption following an unclean shutdown. Latency pattern was similar to the Jul 2026 DB saturation incident (INC-300) but root cause was entirely different — search requests fell back to PostgreSQL full-table scans after Elasticsearch returned partial results. Fixed by rebuilding the Elasticsearch index. Note: surface symptoms identical but root cause different.

title: Catalog API — latency spike from index corruption
content: Catalog search latency exceeded 20 seconds. Root cause: Elasticsearch index corruption after an unexpected node restart. Fallback to PostgreSQL full-table scans caused DB saturation. Different from Jul 2026 incident which was caused by marketing traffic spike, not index corruption. Two incidents with similar latency symptoms but fundamentally different causes.

title: Notification service queue backlog
content: Notification delivery delays exceeded 30 minutes. Root cause: message queue consumer crashed due to an unhandled exception when processing a malformed event payload from orders-api v2.7.8. Queue backlogged with 50,000 messages. Fixed by deploying consumer hotfix and reprocessing queue.

title: Notification service delays — orders-api upstream issue
content: Notification delivery delays on Sep 16 were caused by the orders-api latency spike (INC-1042). Notifications for order confirmations were backed up because order events were not being generated while orders-api was degraded. Not an independent failure — this is a downstream effect of INC-1042.

title: API gateway — elevated error rate Sep 16
content: API gateway recorded elevated 5xx error rate of 12% between 02:15 and 05:30 UTC on Sep 16. Root cause: upstream orders-api latency (INC-1042) caused gateway timeout responses on order-related endpoints. Gateway itself was healthy — this was a cascading effect. Payments and catalog endpoints were unaffected.

title: Customer complaint — general platform slowness Sep 16
content: Enterprise customers reported general platform slowness on Sep 16 morning. Complaints covered order placement, order tracking, and checkout flows. Catalog browsing was unaffected. Root cause was orders-api latency (INC-1042) cascading through the API gateway. 8 enterprise accounts filed formal SLA complaints.

title: Certificate renewal runbook for auth-service
content: Steps to renew auth-service certificates manually: 1. Verify cert expiry date via: kubectl get secret auth-tls-cert -o jsonpath='{.data.tls.crt}' | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -dates 2. Trigger cert-manager renewal: kubectl annotate certificate auth-tls-cert cert-manager.io/issue-temporary-certificate=true 3. Wait for new secret to propagate (typically 2-3 minutes). 4. Perform rolling restart of auth-service pods. 5. Verify TLS handshake success.

title: Catalog API — Elasticsearch index rebuild procedure
content: When Elasticsearch index is corrupted: 1. Do NOT restart catalog-api — this will not fix index corruption and will cause a brief outage. 2. Trigger index rebuild via admin API: POST /admin/rebuild-index. 3. Monitor rebuild progress via Kibana. 4. Rebuild typically takes 15-45 minutes depending on document count. 5. After rebuild, verify search latency returns to baseline. Do not use this procedure for latency caused by DB connection issues — separate runbook applies.

title: Inventory service migration runbook
content: Before running Flyway migrations on inventory-service in production: 1. Check current active connection count vs pool_max_size. 2. If connections > 70% of pool_max_size, schedule migration for off-peak window. 3. Enable migration-mode flag which reduces non-migration query concurrency. 4. Set Flyway lock timeout to 10 minutes to prevent indefinite lock holding. 5. Monitor connection pool metrics during migration. This procedure was created after the Feb 2026 DB saturation incident.

title: Post-PM-211 discussion — DB pool recommendations
content: After the May 2026 orders-api DB saturation incident, team discussed pool configuration. @alice: 'We should never run migrations without a pool headroom check.' @bob: 'PM-211 shows that even a small migration can saturate the pool if traffic is at peak.' @carol: 'Proposal: standardize a pre-migration checklist across all services.' Decision: create company-wide pre-migration checklist. See GUIDE-56 and GUIDE-59.

title: Certificate rotation automation — post-mortem learnings
content: Following auth-service cert expiry (INC-400) and orders-api cert expiry (INC-301), team discussed cert rotation strategy. @dave: 'Both incidents could have been prevented with proactive expiry monitoring.' @eve: 'cert-manager should be trusted but we need an independent alerting layer.' @frank: 'Proposal: add Prometheus alert for any cert expiring in < 30 days across all services.' Action item: implement cert expiry monitoring. See PM-180 and PM-212.

title: v2.8.1 pre-deployment risk assessment
content: Risk discussion for orders-api v2.8.1. Identified risks: 1. Connection pool config changes — pool_max_size increase from 10 to 25. 2. ORM query pattern changes — new async query batching. 3. Migration script included for index on order_items table. Team voted to proceed. No decision to add pre-migration load test. This discussion preceded the Sep 16 incident (INC-1042).

title: Search service — high latency
content: Search service p95 latency exceeded 5 seconds. Root cause: Elasticsearch cluster went into yellow state due to an unassigned shard after a node failure. Search requests were routing to overloaded nodes. No deployment preceded this. Resolved by adding a new Elasticsearch node and rebalancing shards. Distinct from catalog-api Elasticsearch issues — separate cluster.

title: Search service — cold start latency
content: Search service experienced high latency after a scheduled maintenance restart. Root cause: Elasticsearch query cache was cold after restart, causing all queries to do full index scans for approximately 20 minutes. Not an incident per se — expected behavior after restart. Documented for reference so future on-call engineers do not escalate unnecessarily.

title: API gateway — rate limiter misconfiguration
content: API gateway applied incorrect rate limits after a config deployment, blocking legitimate enterprise customers. Root cause: rate limit config file had incorrect IP range for enterprise accounts. No service outage — purely config error. Resolved by reverting rate limit config. Customers unaffected beyond brief 429 errors.

title: API gateway v1.5.0 deployment
content: Gateway v1.5.0 deployed at 16:00 UTC. Added per-service circuit breaker configuration. Updated timeout settings for order endpoints from 5s to 10s to accommodate known orders-api migration windows. Uneventful deployment.

title: Inventory service — API timeout after v3.5.0 deploy
content: Inventory service API timeouts starting 30 minutes after v3.5.0 deployment. Root cause: Flyway migration included in v3.5.0 ran longer than expected on the large stock_movements table, causing connection pool saturation. Same pattern as Feb 2026 incident (INC-600) and PM-211. Resolved by aborting migration and running it off-peak using GUIDE-59 procedure.

title: Inventory service migration saturation postmortem Aug 2026
content: Third occurrence of DB saturation during migration on inventory-service (previous: Feb 2026 INC-600). Root cause: pre-migration checklist (GUIDE-59) was not followed. Engineers ran migration without checking active connection count. Action: make GUIDE-59 checklist a mandatory pre-merge requirement for all PRs containing Flyway migrations.

title: Customer complaint — inventory unavailable Aug 20
content: B2B customers reported inability to check stock availability for approximately 45 minutes on August 20. Mapped to INC-1047. Customers needed to know stock levels for urgent procurement decisions. Escalated to account management.

title: Orders API — latency from Redis cache failure
content: Orders API experienced latency increase after Redis cache cluster became unavailable due to a memory OOM kill. Latency was caused by cache misses forcing all requests to hit the database directly. Root cause: Redis was not sized for the traffic increase following a feature launch. Different from DB connection saturation — DB was handling load but was slower without cache. Resolved by scaling Redis cluster.

title: Orders API — high latency from N+1 query bug
content: Orders API latency spiked after v2.1.0 deployment. Root cause: N+1 query bug introduced in the order history endpoint — each order item triggered a separate database query. Under normal load the impact was masked, but under high traffic the DB was overwhelmed with queries. Different from connection pool saturation — connections were available but queries were inefficient. Fixed in v2.1.1 hotfix.

title: Orders API N+1 query bug postmortem Nov 2023
content: Deployment of v2.1.0 introduced an N+1 query in the order history endpoint. Under high traffic, this generated thousands of DB queries per second. DB connections were not saturated — connection pool metrics were normal. DB CPU spiked to 100%. This incident is distinct from later connection pool saturation incidents (PM-211) — same symptom (latency) but completely different DB-level mechanism.

title: Orders API connection pool configuration guide
content: The orders-api connection pool is configured via DATABASE_POOL_MAX_SIZE and DATABASE_POOL_TIMEOUT environment variables. Default: pool_max_size=10, timeout=30s. Under migration conditions, effective pool availability is reduced by 2-3 connections held by the migration runner. Recommendation: keep pool_max_size >= 15 for production workloads with active migrations. Pool monitoring is exposed at /internal/db-pool-stats endpoint.

title: Company-wide certificate management policy
content: All internal service certificates are managed by cert-manager. Certificate validity: 90 days. Automatic rotation starts at T-30 days. Services must be restarted within the rotation window to pick up new certificates. Services that are not restarted will continue using the old certificate until it expires. Monitoring: Prometheus cert expiry alerts configured for all services. Alert fires at T-14 days if cert has not been renewed. Failure mode: silent if cert-manager RBAC permissions are incorrect (see INC-400).

title: Orders API — post-v2.8.1 incident runbook
content: Created following INC-1042. If orders-api shows latency spike after deployment: 1. Check /internal/db-pool-stats immediately. 2. If pool_active >= pool_max_size * 0.8, escalate to DBA. 3. Check if a Flyway or Alembic migration is running. 4. If migration is running: do NOT restart — use GUIDE-56 (DB connection pool runbook). 5. If no migration and no dependency failure: assess GUIDE-12 restart procedure. 6. Log all findings in the incident report.

title: Payments API — TLS cert rotation discussion
content: @frank: 'ARCH-03 says services need to be restarted within cert rotation window. How are we verifying this?' @grace: 'We rely on cert-manager automated rotation but we saw in auth-service that it can fail silently.' @henry: 'Payments-api and orders-api both have mTLS — both need to be restarted together within the window.' Action: add shared on-call runbook for coordinated cert rotation across mTLS pairs.

title: Orders API — first ever major latency incident
content: First major latency incident for orders-api. P95 latency exceeded 15 seconds. Root cause: unexpected traffic spike (3x normal) after a promotional campaign, combined with a DB that was not scaled for the load. Connection pool exhaustion occurred. This was the original incident that established the connection pool saturation pattern now documented in PM-211. Pool size was doubled as remediation.

title: Orders API first latency incident postmortem — Aug 2022
content: First occurrence of DB connection pool saturation on orders-api. Caused by traffic spike, not migration. This established the pattern that later appeared in PM-211 (migration-induced saturation). Key learning: connection pool is a single point of failure under high concurrency. Recommended increasing pool size and adding pool saturation alerting. Pool alerting was implemented; pool size was increased from 5 to 10.

title: Catalog API — slow queries after stats update
content: Catalog API latency increased after PostgreSQL autovacuum and ANALYZE ran on a large table following a bulk import. Query planner chose suboptimal execution plans briefly. Latency resolved within 20 minutes without intervention as planner statistics stabilized. Not a DB saturation incident — connections were normal. Documented to distinguish from other latency patterns.

title: Notification service — email delivery failures
content: Email notifications failed to deliver for 3 hours. Root cause: SMTP relay credentials expired and were not rotated. Error: authentication failure on SMTP connection. This is a credentials/certificate expiry pattern similar to INC-301 (TLS cert) and INC-400 (mTLS cert) but involving SMTP credentials, not TLS certificates. Resolved by rotating SMTP credentials.

title: Incident pattern analysis — Q3 2026
content: Platform engineering discussion on recurring incident patterns in Q3 2026: 1. DB connection saturation: seen in orders-api (PM-211), inventory-service (INC-600, INC-1047), catalog-api (INC-300 partial). Pattern: migrations or traffic spikes overwhelming pool. 2. Certificate expiry: orders-api (INC-301), auth-service (INC-400). Pattern: cert rotation failure silent. 3. Memory pressure: payments-api (INC-501), orders-api (INC-1044). Pattern: memory leak under sustained load. Each pattern has distinct root cause despite similar latency symptoms.

title: Post-incident analysis — Sep 16 orders-api latency
content: Final analysis of INC-1042: root cause confirmed as DB connection pool exhaustion caused by interaction of two v2.8.1 changes: (1) increased pool_max_size creating more concurrent connections, and (2) new ORM async batch queries generating more connections per request. The Alembic migration ran concurrently, reducing available pool headroom. This is the same mechanism as PM-211 (migration lock + pool saturation) but with an additional contributing factor (ORM query pattern change). Action: update GUIDE-60 with ORM-migration interaction as a risk factor.

title: Cross-service cascade failure runbook
content: When multiple services show degradation simultaneously: 1. Identify the earliest-failing service (likely the root cause). 2. Check API gateway error breakdown by upstream service. 3. Distinguish between independent failures vs. cascading downstream effects. 4. Do NOT attempt to restart all affected services simultaneously — this can cause a cascade restart storm. 5. Resolve root cause service first, then verify downstream services recover automatically.

title: Orders API — elevated error rate from config deploy
content: Orders API returned 500 errors for 15 minutes after a config-only deployment. Root cause: environment variable DATABASE_POOL_MAX_SIZE was accidentally set to 0 in the config deploy, disabling connection pooling entirely. Fixed by reverting the config deploy. No DB saturation — connections were being rejected immediately. This pattern (misconfiguration) is distinct from pool saturation under load.

title: Config deployment — orders-api pool misconfiguration
content: Emergency config deployment at 14:30 UTC to revert DATABASE_POOL_MAX_SIZE=0 set accidentally in previous config push. Config revert deployed at 14:45 UTC. Service recovered within 2 minutes of config revert. Root cause of misconfiguration: copy-paste error in config template.

title: Customer complaint — order placement errors Apr 20
content: Customers reported order placement failures showing internal server errors for approximately 15 minutes on April 20. Mapped to INC-1053. Errors were caused by misconfiguration, not service overload. Short duration limited impact to approximately 200 failed order attempts.

title: Payments API — intermittent timeouts after v4.2.0
content: Intermittent payment processing timeouts starting 4 hours after v4.2.0 deployment. Root cause: new payment retry logic introduced in v4.2.0 had an exponential backoff bug — retries were consuming thread pool capacity under sustained failure conditions. Different from memory leak (INC-501) or DB saturation (INC-700) — thread pool exhaustion, not memory or DB. Resolved by deploying hotfix v4.2.1.

title: Payments API — thread pool exhaustion runbook
content: When payments-api shows timeout errors and thread pool metrics show saturation: 1. Check /actuator/metrics/executor.active and executor.pool.size. 2. If active threads == max pool size, thread pool is exhausted. 3. Identify which operation is holding threads (retry storms are a common cause). 4. If retry storm is in progress, temporarily disable retry via feature flag: PAYMENT_RETRY_ENABLED=false. 5. This is distinct from DB connection saturation and memory pressure — separate runbooks apply for those.

title: Search service — index out of sync
content: Search results showed stale data for 6 hours. Root cause: Elasticsearch indexer job failed silently after a Redis connection error caused the job's offset tracking to reset. The indexer restarted from offset 0 and began overwriting current data with stale data. Not a latency incident — search was fast but returning wrong results. Resolved by stopping indexer, restoring from snapshot, and resuming from correct offset.

title: API gateway — SSL certificate mismatch
content: API gateway rejected requests from a subset of enterprise customers with SSL certificate errors. Root cause: gateway was configured with an old certificate for a recently migrated domain. Customers using the new domain endpoint received SSL mismatch errors. Different from internal service certificate expiry (INC-301, INC-400) — this is a customer-facing SSL misconfiguration. Resolved by updating gateway certificate bundle.

title: Notification service architecture overview
content: Notification service consumes events from an Amazon SQS queue published by orders-api, payments-api, and catalog-api. Processes: email (via SMTP relay), push notification (via FCM), and in-app notification (via WebSocket). Known dependencies: SMTP relay credentials (90-day rotation), FCM API key (annual rotation), Redis for WebSocket session tracking. Queue processing is idempotent — duplicate events are safe. Max processing rate: 1,000 events/minute.

title: Search service architecture overview
content: Search service is a Python service backed by Elasticsearch 8.x. Maintains a near-real-time index synced from the catalog database via a Kafka consumer. Indexer tracks offsets in Redis. Known risk: if Redis becomes unavailable, offset tracking is lost and indexer may reprocess from an old offset. Two Elasticsearch clusters: search-cluster-a (primary search) and search-cluster-b (analytics). INC-1045 and INC-1046 both involved search-cluster-a.

title: API gateway architecture overview
content: API gateway is an Nginx-based service with custom Lua plugins for authentication and rate limiting. Routes traffic to: orders-api, catalog-api, payments-api, auth-service, search-service. Circuit breakers configured per upstream. Timeout defaults: 10s for orders-api (extended post INC-1042), 5s for all others. SSL termination at gateway — internal traffic uses mTLS. Rate limiting: 100 req/s per enterprise customer, 10 req/s per free tier.

title: Elasticsearch recovery procedures
content: For Elasticsearch cluster issues: yellow state (unassigned shards) — add a node or reduce replica count. Red state (missing primary shards) — restore from snapshot. Index corruption — rebuild index from source data (see GUIDE-58 for catalog-api specific procedure). Cold cache after restart — allow 15-20 minutes for cache warmup before declaring an incident. Do not use this procedure for issues caused by the Kafka consumer or Redis offset tracking — separate runbook applies.

title: Orders API — high latency from slow external payment API
content: Orders API p95 latency climbed to 12 seconds. Root cause: external payment provider API was responding slowly (15-20 second response times). Orders-api was waiting synchronously for payment authorization before completing order placement. No internal failure. Resolved when payment provider recovered. This latency incident has an external cause — not a deployment, DB, memory, or certificate issue.

title: Discussion — async payment authorization
content: Following INC-1057 where external payment slowness caused orders-api latency: @alice: 'We should make payment authorization async to prevent external provider slowness from affecting orders-api latency.' @bob: 'Agreed, but we need to handle the case where payment fails after order is created.' @carol: 'This is a significant architecture change — add to roadmap but not immediate fix.' Deferred to Q3 2025 roadmap.

title: Inventory service — latency from Redis unavailability
content: Inventory service latency increased when Redis became unavailable due to an OOM kill. Inventory service uses Redis for rate limiting counters — without Redis, rate limiting fell back to in-memory counters which were not shared across instances, allowing traffic bursts. No connection pool saturation — DB was performing normally. Redis was restarted to resolve. Similar Redis OOM pattern to orders-api Redis incident (INC-1048) but on different service and different Redis usage.

title: Postmortem — Sep 16 orders-api latency spike (INC-1042)
content: Full root cause analysis: INC-1042 was caused by DB connection pool exhaustion. Contributing factors: (1) v2.8.1 increased pool_max_size from 10 to 25, creating higher connection concurrency. (2) New ORM async query batching in v2.8.1 generated more connections per request than previous version. (3) Alembic migration ran concurrently at peak traffic, consuming pool headroom. The combination of factors 1+2+3 overwhelmed the DB. Previous incident PM-211 had the same pool saturation mechanism but was caused by migration alone without the ORM change factor. Recommendation: run v2.8.1 ORM changes separately from migration in future deployments.

title: DB connection pool saturation — company-wide runbook
content: Applies to: orders-api, inventory-service, catalog-api, payments-api, auth-service. Symptoms: request timeouts, connection refused errors, pool_active == pool_max_size. Step 1: identify if a migration is running (check migration logs). Step 2: if migration is running, do NOT restart — use service-specific migration runbook. Step 3: if no migration, check if a query-level issue is causing connection hold (slow queries, N+1 patterns). Step 4: if traffic spike is cause, scale read replicas. Step 5: if pool_max_size needs emergency increase, use runtime config API (service-specific). This runbook does NOT apply to latency caused by certificate expiry, memory pressure, or external dependency slowness.

title: Payments API — latency from DB index missing
content: Payments API experienced high latency on payment history queries after a hotfix deployment. Root cause: hotfix included a DB migration that accidentally dropped an index on the payment_transactions table. Without the index, payment history queries performed full table scans on a 200M-row table. DB connection pool was not saturated — query volume was normal but each query was much slower. Fixed by recreating the index.

title: Auth service — slow login after Redis upgrade
content: Auth service login latency increased from 50ms to 800ms after Redis upgrade. Root cause: new Redis version changed default serialization format causing deserialization overhead. Not a DB connection issue or certificate issue — auth-service was healthy, Redis was healthy, but the serialization mismatch caused CPU overhead. Resolved by configuring Redis to use the previous serialization format.

title: Auth service v6.1.0 deployment — Redis upgrade
content: Auth service v6.1.0 deployed at 11:00 UTC. Key change: upgraded Redis client library from v4 to v5 with new serialization format. Smoke tests passed in staging with fresh Redis data. Note: staging Redis did not have production data serialized in old format — this mismatch was not caught in staging. Latency issue (INC-1060) appeared 4 hours after deployment once production Redis sessions began deserializing.

title: Customer complaint — slow login Aug 25
content: Users reported sluggish login experience on August 25. Login took 5-10 seconds instead of the usual under 1 second. Mapped to INC-1060 (Redis serialization overhead). High volume of complaints from mobile app users who had shorter tolerance for slow authentication. No authentication failures — just slowness.

title: Orders API — no incident post v2.8.2 deployment
content: Orders API v2.8.2 was deployed on Oct 1. This version separated the ORM query pattern changes from any DB migration (lessons from INC-1042). Deployment was monitored with enhanced DB pool metrics. No connection pool saturation observed. P95 latency remained at baseline throughout. Deployment declared successful after 24-hour monitoring window.

title: Orders API v2.8.2 deployment — post-INC-1042 improvements
content: v2.8.2 deployed following PM-216 recommendations. Changes: (1) ORM query optimizations now use bounded connection acquisition to prevent pool exhaustion. (2) Alembic migration split into a separate maintenance window. (3) Added /internal/db-pool-stats alert if pool_active > 80% pool_max_size. Deployment monitoring: enhanced for 48 hours post-deploy. No incidents.

title: Orders API v2.8+ deployment checklist
content: Before deploying orders-api v2.8.x or later: 1. Separate any DB migrations into an independent maintenance window. 2. Verify pool_max_size is set to 20 or higher (not 10 — the pre-v2.8 default was too low). 3. Check ORM async batch query setting: ENABLE_ASYNC_BATCH=true is the high-risk config — verify with DBA if changing. 4. Post-deploy: monitor /internal/db-pool-stats for first 2 hours. 5. Have GUIDE-56 (DB pool runbook) and GUIDE-60 open during deployment. This checklist was created after INC-1042 and PM-216.

title: Catalog API — search degradation from Elasticsearch OOM
content: Catalog search degraded for 45 minutes after Elasticsearch node went OOM and was killed. Remaining nodes handled traffic but with reduced capacity. Root cause: Elasticsearch heap was sized for 3 nodes but one node had been running with elevated heap usage due to an unmerged segment. This is an infrastructure-level failure, not a deployment or DB issue. Resolved by restarting the OOM-killed node with reduced JVM heap settings.

title: Notification service — SQS message processing delay
content: Notification processing delayed by 45 minutes for order confirmation emails. Root cause: SQS queue had a misconfigured visibility timeout of 30 seconds — messages were becoming visible again before processing completed, causing repeated processing attempts and queue backlog. Not related to upstream service failures — orders-api was healthy. Fixed by increasing visibility timeout to 5 minutes.

title: Customer complaint — no order confirmation email
content: Multiple customers complained about not receiving order confirmation emails after placing orders. Orders were successfully placed but email notifications were delayed by 45 minutes due to SQS misconfiguration (INC-1063). Customers were worried their orders had not gone through and contacted support.

title: Incident retrospective — Q3/Q4 2026 patterns
content: Platform reliability review for Q3/Q4 2026. Recurring patterns: 1. DB connection pool saturation continues despite runbooks — enforcement gap. 2. Certificate expiry incidents reduced after ARCH-07 monitoring implementation. 3. Configuration-level incidents (INC-1053, INC-901, INC-1063) suggest deployment process needs config validation step. 4. Memory pressure incidents declining as teams adopt heap monitoring. Action: mandatory config validation in CI/CD pipeline before any config deployment.

title: General incident triage checklist
content: When an incident is reported: 1. Identify the affected service(s) and whether impact is isolated or cascading. 2. Check if a deployment preceded the incident (within 24 hours). 3. Check DB connection pool metrics. 4. Check memory and CPU metrics. 5. Check certificate expiry dates. 6. Check upstream dependencies. Based on findings, refer to service-specific runbook. Do not assume the cause — verify metrics before acting. Restarting a service should be the LAST resort, not the first action.

title: Orders API — latency from third-party fraud check API slowness
content: Orders API latency elevated for 2 hours due to third-party fraud detection API responding slowly. Orders-api calls the fraud API synchronously before confirming orders. When fraud API slowed, orders-api response times increased proportionally. Root cause is entirely external. No internal failure. Resolved when fraud API provider resolved their issue. This is the second instance of external API slowness causing orders-api latency (see also INC-1057 — payment provider slowness).

title: Orders API — external dependency risk assessment
content: Orders-api has three synchronous external dependencies: (1) payments-api (internal), (2) fraud detection API (external, third-party), (3) tax calculation API (external, third-party). Any of these becoming slow will directly increase orders-api response times. Recommendation: implement circuit breakers and async handoff for external dependencies. Current state: payments-api has circuit breaker; fraud and tax APIs do not. INC-1057 and INC-1064 both resulted from missing circuit breakers on external dependencies.

title: Payments API — DB read latency after storage migration
content: Payments API DB read latency tripled after a storage migration moved the RDS instance to a new availability zone. Network latency between the application tier and the new AZ added 40ms per DB round trip. Not a connection pool issue — pool was healthy. Latency was from increased network RTT. Resolved by migrating application tier to the same AZ as the new RDS instance.

title: Auth service — JWT issuance failure from clock skew
content: JWT token issuance failed for 20 minutes due to a clock skew issue. NTP synchronization failed on the auth-service host causing the system clock to drift by 90 seconds. JWTs were being issued with a past expiry time, causing immediate rejection. Root cause: NTP daemon crashed silently. No deployment preceded this. Fixed by restarting NTP and syncing clock. Clock monitoring added post-incident.

title: Customer complaint — unable to log in Jul 10
content: Users reported being immediately logged out after logging in or unable to complete login. Auth tokens were invalid on issuance due to clock skew (INC-1066). Enterprise users attempting to use API tokens were also affected. Duration: 20 minutes. Resolved after clock sync. Apology email sent to affected enterprise customers.

title: Search service — elevated latency post v1.3.0
content: Search service p95 latency increased from 200ms to 1.2 seconds after v1.3.0 deployment. Root cause: new query rewriting feature in v1.3.0 was generating complex Elasticsearch queries that were not optimized for the current index mapping. No Elasticsearch cluster issues — all nodes healthy. Fixed by disabling the query rewriting feature flag and scheduling a performance optimization sprint.

title: Orders API — 500 errors from database schema mismatch
content: Orders API returned 500 errors after a partial deployment. Root cause: database schema migration ran ahead of the application deployment, causing the running v2.2.0 code to query columns that had been renamed in the migration. Errors resolved after v2.3.0 deployment completed. No latency issue — errors were immediate. This is a deployment ordering problem, not a performance issue.

title: Deployment ordering — zero-downtime migration guide
content: To prevent schema mismatch errors (INC-1068 pattern): 1. Migrations must be backward-compatible with the previous code version. 2. Add new columns before renaming/removing old ones. 3. Deploy application code that reads both old and new column names. 4. Then run rename/removal migration. 5. Then remove backward compatibility code in next deploy. This is the expand-contract migration pattern. Failure to follow this caused INC-1068.

title: Postmortem — schema mismatch 500 errors Jun 2024
content: 500 errors on orders-api caused by migration running before deployment completed. Root cause: blue-green deployment timing meant the migration ran against blue environment before green environment was fully deployed. Fix: enforce expand-contract pattern (GUIDE-67). This is a different incident class from latency/performance issues — no connection pool saturation, no certificate expiry. Immediate errors, not gradual degradation.

title: Inventory service — API latency from Flyway lock timeout
content: Inventory API latency spiked during a Flyway migration that exceeded the 10-minute lock timeout. The lock timeout caused the migration to fail, but Flyway held the lock briefly during failure handling, causing requests to queue. After the lock was released, service recovered. No connection pool saturation — the brief lock hold caused temporary request queuing, not pool exhaustion. Migration was rescheduled to a maintenance window.

title: Discussion — Flyway migration incident patterns on inventory-service
content: Third migration-related incident on inventory-service in 3 months. @ivan: 'We keep running into Flyway issues. GUIDE-59 exists but is not consistently followed.' @jane: 'The pre-migration checklist needs to be enforced in CI, not just documented.' @kevin: 'We should gate Flyway migration PRs behind a mandatory DBA review.' Decision: add DBA sign-off as a required approval for any PR containing a Flyway migration affecting large tables (> 1M rows).

title: How to distinguish DB saturation from DB slowness
content: DB connection pool saturation and DB query slowness are both latency causes but require different responses. Saturation: pool_active == pool_max_size, new requests queue or fail with connection timeout. Query slowness: pool metrics normal, but individual query duration is high (check slow query log). Key diagnostic: check pool_active metric first. If saturation: use DB pool runbook (GUIDE-64). If pool is healthy but queries are slow: check for missing indexes, N+1 patterns, table bloat, or missing ANALYZE statistics. Do not conflate these — different causes, different fixes.

title: Orders API — latency from missing composite index
content: Orders API order history endpoint latency increased from 80ms to 3 seconds after a DB schema change removed a composite index unintentionally. Root cause: a migration in v2.7.7 dropped a composite index on (customer_id, created_at) while adding a new index on (order_status, created_at). The removed index was used by the order history query. DB connection pool was not saturated — queries were slow, not failing to connect. Fixed by adding back the composite index.

title: Postmortem — missing index latency Jul 2026
content: INC-1070: composite index accidentally dropped during migration. Latency increased due to full table scans on orders table. Mechanism distinct from connection pool saturation (PM-211) — pool was healthy, queries were slow. Detection delay: 4 hours because pool saturation was assumed first (wrong assumption). Recommendation: add query duration SLO monitoring in addition to connection pool monitoring. Pattern same as PM-100 (N+1 queries) in terms of mechanism — DB load without pool saturation.

title: Payments API — no incident post v4.2.1 deployment
content: Payments API v4.2.1 hotfix deployed on Sep 14 to fix the retry logic bug (INC-1054). Deployment was monitored for 12 hours. Thread pool metrics remained healthy. No timeouts observed. Payment processing returned to normal error rates. Deployment declared successful.

title: Customer complaint — slow product search Sep 21
content: Enterprise customers reported search results taking 3-5 seconds after the v1.3.0 deployment. Mapped to INC-1067 (Elasticsearch query rewriting feature). Customers on the premium tier especially affected as they use complex search queries that were most impacted by the rewriting logic. Issue resolved after feature flag was disabled.

title: Catalog API — 404 errors from config mismatch
content: Catalog API returned 404 for all product endpoints for 10 minutes after a config deployment. Root cause: database connection string in config pointed to a non-existent database name due to a typo. Application could not connect to DB and returned 404 for all data-dependent endpoints. Not a latency issue — immediate failures. Fixed by correcting the connection string and redeploying config.

title: Platform reliability — known failure patterns
content: Documented failure patterns as of Sep 2026: (1) DB connection pool saturation: orders-api, inventory-service, auth-service, payments-api all vulnerable. Root cause: migrations or traffic spikes under-sized pools. (2) Certificate expiry: orders-api, auth-service affected. Risk ongoing. (3) Memory leaks: orders-api (v2.5.0), payments-api (v3.9.0) patterns. (4) External dependency slowness: orders-api vulnerable (fraud API, payment provider). (5) Configuration errors: catalog-api, orders-api, gateway-api affected. (6) Index/query performance: orders-api (N+1, missing indexes). Each pattern has distinct diagnostics — do not treat similar symptoms as same root cause.

title: Orders API — recovery and validation Sep 16
content: Following INC-1042, orders-api was stabilized at 06:00 UTC on Sep 16 by DBA intervention: connection pool was flushed and pool_max_size was temporarily reduced to prevent saturation recurrence. Service monitored for 4 hours post-stabilization. No recurrence. v2.8.1 remained deployed but with modified pool configuration. Full fix deployed in v2.8.2 (DEP-885) on Oct 1.

title: INC-1042 timeline and recovery postmortem
content: Timeline: Sep 15 18:10 UTC: v2.8.1 deployed (DEP-882). Sep 15 23:40 UTC: Alembic migration starts. Sep 16 02:15 UTC: DB connection pool saturates, latency spikes (INC-1042). Sep 16 02:30 UTC: on-call paged, customer complaints start (CC-10). Sep 16 04:00 UTC: DBA engaged, pool analysis completed. Sep 16 06:00 UTC: pool flushed, service stabilized (INC-1073). Sep 16 06:30 UTC: notification service delays attributed to upstream (INC-801). Total customer-visible impact: ~4 hours. Lessons: pre-migration pool check would have caught this, per ENG-01 pre-deploy discussion.

title: Inventory service — not affected Sep 16
content: Inventory service was monitored during the Sep 16 orders-api incident. Inventory service remained healthy throughout. No connection pool saturation, no latency increase, no customer impact. Orders-api DB saturation did not cascade to inventory-service because the two services use independent database clusters. This document confirms that INC-1042 was isolated to orders-api infrastructure.

title: Enterprise SLA breach report — Sep 16
content: Formal SLA breach report filed by 3 enterprise customers following INC-1042. Orders-api was below the 99.9% availability SLA for the calendar month due to the 4-hour incident. Customers requesting SLA credits. Account management engaged. Postmortem PM-219 shared with enterprise customers as transparency measure.

title: Platform-wide action items from Sep 16 incident
content: Following INC-1042 and PM-216/219, platform-wide action items: 1. All services must run DB migrations in separate maintenance windows from feature deployments. 2. All services must add DB pool saturation alerting at 80% threshold. 3. Connection pool size must be reviewed before any deployment that changes query patterns. 4. DBA sign-off required for any migration on tables > 5M rows. 5. Update GUIDE-64 with new thresholds. These actions generalize the lessons of INC-1042 across the platform, recognizing that the DB saturation pattern is not unique to orders-api (see: inventory-service INC-600, INC-1047, payments-api INC-700).

  {"document_id":"ARCH-08","type":"architecture_note","service":"notification-service","date":"2026-03-01","version":"v2.x","title":"Notification service architecture overview","content":"Notification service consumes events from an Amazon SQS queue published by orders-api, payments-api, and catalog-api.   {"document_id":"ARCH-09","type":"architecture_note","service":"search-service","date":"2026-02-01","version":"v1.x","title":"Search service architecture overview","content":"Search service is a Python service backed by Elasticsearch 8.x.   {"document_id":"ARCH-10","type":"architecture_note","service":"gateway-api","date":"2026-06-01","version":"v1.5.x","title":"API gateway architecture overview","content":"API gateway is an Nginx-based service with custom Lua plugins for authentication and rate limiting.   {"document_id":"GUIDE-63","type":"troubleshooting","service":null,"date":"2026-04-01","version":"v3","title":"Elasticsearch recovery procedures","content":"For Elasticsearch cluster issues: yellow state (unassigned shards) — add a node or reduce replica count.   {"document_id":"INC-1057","type":"incident_report","service":"orders-api","date":"2025-06-15","version":"v2.6.2","title":"Orders API — high latency from slow external payment API","content":"Orders API p95 latency climbed to 12 seconds.   {"document_id":"ENG-09","type":"engineering_discussion","service":"orders-api","date":"2025-06-17","version":null,"title":"Discussion — async payment authorization","content":"Following INC-1057 where external payment slowness caused orders-api latency: @alice: 'We should make payment authorization async to prevent external provider slowness from affecting orders-api latency.' @bob: 'Agreed, but we need to handle the case where payment fails after order is created.' @carol: 'This is a significant architecture change — add to roadmap but not immediate fix.'   {"document_id":"INC-1058","type":"incident_report","service":"inventory-service","date":"2025-09-20","version":"v3.3.0","title":"Inventory service — latency from Redis unavailability","content":"Inventory service latency increased when Redis became unavailable due to an OOM kill.   {"document_id":"PM-216","type":"postmortem","service":"orders-api","date":"2026-09-19","version":"v2.8.1","title":"Postmortem — Sep 16 orders-api latency spike (INC-1042)","content":"Full root cause analysis: INC-1042 was caused by DB connection pool exhaustion. Contributing factors: (1) v2.8.1 increased pool_max_size from 10 to 25, creating higher connection concurrency. (2) New ORM async query batching in v2.8.1 generated more connections per request than previous version. (3) Alembic migration ran concurrently at peak traffic, consuming pool headroom. The combination of factors 1+2+3 overwhelmed the DB. Previous incident PM-211 had the same pool saturation mechanism but was caused by migration alone without the ORM change factor. Recommendation: run v2.8.1 ORM changes separately from migration in future deployments."},
  {"document_id":"GUIDE-64","type":"troubleshooting","service":null,"date":"2026-09-18","version":"v1","title":"DB connection pool saturation — company-wide runbook","content":"Applies to: orders-api, inventory-service, catalog-api, payments-api, auth-service. Symptoms: request timeouts, connection refused errors, pool_active == pool_max_size. Step 1: identify if a migration is running (check migration logs). Step 2: if migration is running, do NOT restart — use service-specific migration runbook. Step 3: if no migration, check if a query-level issue is causing connection hold (slow queries, N+1 patterns). Step 4: if traffic spike is cause, scale read replicas. Step 5: if pool_max_size needs emergency increase, use runtime config API (service-specific). This runbook does NOT apply to latency caused by certificate expiry, memory pressure, or external dependency slowness."},
  {"document_id":"INC-1059","type":"incident_report","service":"payments-api","date":"2026-05-15","version":"v3.9.2","title":"Payments API — latency from DB index missing","content":"Payments API experienced high latency on payment history queries after a hotfix deployment.   {"document_id":"INC-1060","type":"incident_report","service":"auth-service","date":"2026-08-25","version":"v6.1.0","title":"Auth service — slow login after Redis upgrade","content":"Auth service login latency increased from 50ms to 800ms after Redis upgrade.   {"document_id":"DEP-610","type":"deployment_note","service":"auth-service","date":"2026-08-24","version":"v6.1.0","title":"Auth service v6.1.0 deployment — Redis upgrade","content":"Auth service v6.1.0 deployed at 11:00 UTC.   {"document_id":"DEP-885","type":"deployment_note","service":"orders-api","date":"2026-10-01","version":"v2.8.2","title":"Orders API v2.8.2 deployment — post-INC-1042 improvements","content":"v2.8.2 deployed following PM-216 recommendations.   {"document_id":"GUIDE-65","type":"troubleshooting","service":"orders-api","date":"2026-10-02","version":"v6","title":"Orders API v2.8+ deployment checklist","content":"Before deploying orders-api v2.8.x or later: 1. Have GUIDE-56 (DB pool runbook) and GUIDE-60 open during deployment. This checklist was created after INC-1042 and PM-216."},
  {"document_id":"INC-1062","type":"incident_report","service":"catalog-api","date":"2026-10-05","version":"v5.3","title":"Catalog API — search degradation from Elasticsearch OOM","content":"Catalog search degraded for 45 minutes after Elasticsearch node went OOM and was killed.   {"document_id":"INC-1063","type":"incident_report","service":"notification-service","date":"2026-10-08","version":"v2.3.0","title":"Notification service — SQS message processing delay","content":"Notification processing delayed by 45 minutes for order confirmation emails.   {"document_id":"ENG-10","type":"engineering_discussion","service":null,"date":"2026-10-10","version":null,"title":"Incident retrospective — Q3/Q4 2026 patterns","content":"Platform reliability review for Q3/Q4 2026. Recurring patterns: 1. DB connection pool saturation continues despite runbooks — enforcement gap. 2. Certificate expiry incidents reduced after ARCH-07 monitoring implementation. 3. Configuration-level incidents (INC-1053, INC-901, INC-1063) suggest deployment process needs config validation step. 4. Memory pressure incidents declining as teams adopt heap monitoring.   {"document_id":"GUIDE-66","type":"troubleshooting","service":null,"date":"2026-10-01","version":"v1","title":"General incident triage checklist","content":"When an incident is reported: 1.   {"document_id":"INC-1064","type":"incident_report","service":"orders-api","date":"2026-06-30","version":"v2.7.5","title":"Orders API — latency from third-party fraud check API slowness","content":"Orders API latency elevated for 2 hours due to third-party fraud detection API responding slowly.   {"document_id":"ARCH-11","type":"architecture_note","service":"orders-api","date":"2026-07-15","version":"v2.8.x","title":"Orders API — external dependency risk assessment","content":"Orders-api has three synchronous external dependencies: (1) payments-api (internal), (2) fraud detection API (external, third-party), (3) tax calculation API (external, third-party).   {"document_id":"INC-1065","type":"incident_report","service":"payments-api","date":"2026-03-18","version":"v4.0.0","title":"Payments API — DB read latency after storage migration","content":"Payments API DB read latency tripled after a storage migration moved the RDS instance to a new availability zone.   {"document_id":"CC-45","type":"customer_complaint","service":"auth-service","date":"2025-07-10","version":null,"title":"Customer complaint — unable to log in Jul 10","content":"Users reported being immediately logged out after logging in or unable to complete login.   {"document_id":"INC-1067","type":"incident_report","service":"search-service","date":"2026-09-20","version":"v1.3.0","title":"Search service — elevated latency post v1.3.0","content":"Search service p95 latency increased from 200ms to 1.2 seconds after v1.3.0 deployment.   {"document_id":"INC-1068","type":"incident_report","service":"orders-api","date":"2024-06-22","version":"v2.3.0","title":"Orders API — 500 errors from database schema mismatch","content":"Orders API returned 500 errors after a partial deployment.   {"document_id":"GUIDE-67","type":"troubleshooting","service":null,"date":"2024-07-01","version":"v1","title":"Deployment ordering — zero-downtime migration guide","content":"To prevent schema mismatch errors (INC-1068 pattern): 1. Migrations must be backward-compatible with the previous code version. 2. Add new columns before renaming/removing old ones. 3. Deploy application code that reads both old and new column names. 4. Then run rename/removal migration. 5. Then remove backward compatibility code in next deploy. This is the expand-contract migration pattern. Failure to follow this caused INC-1068."},
  {"document_id":"PM-217","type":"postmortem","service":"orders-api","date":"2024-06-24","version":"v2.3.0","title":"Postmortem — schema mismatch 500 errors Jun 2024","content":"500 errors on orders-api caused by migration running before deployment completed.   {"document_id":"INC-1069","type":"incident_report","service":"inventory-service","date":"2026-05-14","version":"v3.4.5","title":"Inventory service — API latency from Flyway lock timeout","content":"Inventory API latency spiked during a Flyway migration that exceeded the 10-minute lock timeout.   {"document_id":"ENG-11","type":"engineering_discussion","service":"inventory-service","date":"2026-05-16","version":null,"title":"Discussion — Flyway migration incident patterns on inventory-service","content":"Third migration-related incident on inventory-service in 3 months. @ivan: 'We keep running into Flyway issues.   {"document_id":"GUIDE-68","type":"troubleshooting","service":null,"date":"2026-06-01","version":"v2","title":"How to distinguish DB saturation from DB slowness","content":"DB connection pool saturation and DB query slowness are both latency causes but require different responses. Saturation: pool_active == pool_max_size, new requests queue or fail with connection timeout. Query slowness: pool metrics normal, but individual query duration is high (check slow query log). Key diagnostic: check pool_active metric first. If saturation: use DB pool runbook (GUIDE-64). If pool is healthy but queries are slow: check for missing indexes, N+1 patterns, table bloat, or missing ANALYZE statistics. Do not conflate these — different causes, different fixes."},
  {"document_id":"INC-1070","type":"incident_report","service":"orders-api","date":"2026-07-08","version":"v2.7.7","title":"Orders API — latency from missing composite index","content":"Orders API order history endpoint latency increased from 80ms to 3 seconds after a DB schema change removed a composite index unintentionally.   {"document_id":"PM-218","type":"postmortem","service":"orders-api","date":"2026-07-10","version":"v2.7.7","title":"Postmortem — missing index latency Jul 2026","content":"INC-1070: composite index accidentally dropped during migration.   {"document_id":"INC-1071","type":"incident_report","service":"payments-api","date":"2026-09-14","version":"v4.2.1","title":"Payments API — no incident post v4.2.1 deployment","content":"Payments API v4.2.1 hotfix deployed on Sep 14 to fix the retry logic bug (INC-1054).   {"document_id":"CC-46","type":"customer_complaint","service":"search-service","date":"2026-09-21","version":null,"title":"Customer complaint — slow product search Sep 21","content":"Enterprise customers reported search results taking 3-5 seconds after the v1.3.0 deployment.   {"document_id":"INC-1072","type":"incident_report","service":"catalog-api","date":"2025-08-10","version":"v4.8","title":"Catalog API — 404 errors from config mismatch","content":"Catalog API returned 404 for all product endpoints for 10 minutes after a config deployment.   {"document_id":"ARCH-12","type":"architecture_note","service":null,"date":"2026-09-01","version":null,"title":"Platform reliability — known failure patterns","content":"Documented failure patterns as of Sep 2026: (1) DB connection pool saturation: orders-api, inventory-service, auth-service, payments-api all vulnerable.   {"document_id":"PM-219","type":"postmortem","service":"orders-api","date":"2026-09-18","version":"v2.8.1","title":"INC-1042 timeline and recovery postmortem","content":"Timeline: Sep 15 18:10 UTC: v2.8.1 deployed (DEP-882).   {"document_id":"CC-47","type":"customer_complaint","service":"orders-api","date":"2026-09-16","version":null,"title":"Enterprise SLA breach report — Sep 16","content":"Formal SLA breach report filed by 3 enterprise customers following INC-1042.   {"document_id":"ENG-12","type":"engineering_discussion","service":null,"date":"2026-09-20","version":null,"title":"Platform-wide action items from Sep 16 incident","content":"Following INC-1042 and PM-216/219, platform-wide action items: 1. title: Order API failure due to upstream
content: The order-api began failing at 10:00 AM UTC. Initial investigations revealed that the failures are due to an upstream timeout in the payment-service. The order-api itself is healthy, but cannot complete transactions without the payment-service.

title: Payment Service v3.0 Deployment
content: Version 3.0 of the payment-service was deployed at 09:50 AM UTC. This deployment included a new fraud detection algorithm which has been observed to cause significant latency spikes and timeouts under load. A rollback is being considered.
